Even the Chinese government, which owns the longtime paraquat maker Syngenta, halted domestic use of the pesticide a decade ago after conducting its own studies on paraquat safety and finding troubling results.

In the US, two states – Vermont and California – have recently also banned paraquat, citing risks that include an association between paraquat and Parkinson’s disease shown in years of scientific research. item.title: Don’t let the age of AI make you forget the B2B buyer is human
item.description:
Today, as I look across tech, industrial, and professional services, I see hundreds of companies doing extraordinary work. However, far too often, their most persuasive, human stories are hidden from current and prospective customers.

I see marketing leaders holding onto outdated assumptions about why B2B buyers really make decisions. And I see executives, marketers, and customers missing the point about what AI does well and what it can never replace.

It’s clear that B2B marketers have never had more sophisticated tools at their disposal. Here are three myths they need to bust if they want to get the most out of those tools, and the people who use them.

Myth #1: Long sales cycles can be measured with short-term metrics

B2B purchases are frequently made by multiple decision-makers, after extensive research, over months or even years of consideration. Yet the marketing to influence them is often managed by short-term metrics.

The key to better B2B sales outcomes—and better decision-making along the way—is to focus on what matters most in long-haul buying cycles: creating a memorable brand.

When I was at GE, where long cycle was the name of the game, the goal was not to explain every technical detail in our marketing. It was to create meaning and differentiation so future customers knew and trusted GE. 

Had we measured ourselves on the number of demos requested or clicks to our site, we’d have targeted only the comparatively small number of buyers in the market for a solution rather than influencing buyers for the long term. 

With this north star always in mind, we made early bets on new platforms, channels, and storytelling formats.

Long before the creator economy, we invited popular YouTubers to come to our historic Global Research Center and tell the story of a new material coating using slow-motion photography. 

We won our first Cannes Lion for a simple user-generated content campaign on Vine, the short-form video predecessor to TikTok. 

And we created a chart-topping, eight-episode sci-fi thriller podcast long before “branded entertainment” was a popular concept. 

None of these efforts were designed to replace product marketing. But every one of them, and scores of others, created a memorable and emotional framework that reinforced GE’s history and future promise of innovation.  

Myth #2: Buying is a purely rational decision

Long before chief marketing officers were saying that brands needed to be “authentic,” a handful of big companies showed up in American households as a person, not simply as a company. In the 1940s, the silver screen star Betty Furness demonstrated Westinghouse appliances on TV, humanizing the brand for millions of American women. Ronald Reagan and GE took it a step further with General Electric Theater in the 1950s. And by the ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s, TV commercial breaks were full of celebrities lending their warmth and charm to financial services, automotive, consumer products, and eventually technology companies who wanted their brand to inspire emotions. 

That principle shaped how we kept the GE brand relevant and fresh. We didn’t focus on the turbine, but the power it generated for homes. We didn’t talk about healthcare technology, but the patient lives it saved. Whenever we could, we made the story about people.

Many B2B executives don’t see the opportunity or value in appealing to buyers on an emotional level. But when businesses and brands communicate like manuals or faceless corporate giants instead of people, they’re leaving money on the table. 

Gartner reports that B2B buyers are nearly three times as likely to demonstrate high brand commitment when they perceive personal benefits from a supplier rather than functional benefits alone. Research by Les Binet and Peter Field for LinkedIn’s B2B Institute similarly found that emotional B2B campaigns generated seven times as many “very large business effects” over the long term as campaigns built primarily around rational appeals. Appealing to the emotions is very, very good for business.

Myth #3: AI makes brand storytelling less important

When an artificial intelligence assistant can compare specifications, features, and create detailed summaries of a company’s claims before the buyer ever visits a supplier’s website, what’s left to sway a B2B buyer? The brand story that a company has built up over time.

Product marketing, defined as the battle of specifications between niche products, will always be important, especially since AI needs an endless supply of fresh data to feed on. But for the human on the other side of the screen, brand association is now more likely than ever to cast the deciding vote.

Generative AI works by identifying patterns in what already exists and repeating them. Brand differentiation works the opposite way. It requires departing from those patterns at precisely the right moment, as only a human being can determine.

AI can provide an endless stream of ideas, but only human decision-making, born of experience, creativity, empathy and a deep understanding of the brand, can know what to do with them.

As more organizations use the same AI tools to conduct research, develop strategies and generate content, the danger is growing that brands will go down the algorithmic middle road: safe, efficient, and entirely forgettable.

By all means, use AI to accelerate research, production and adaptation. But please, do not ask it to decide what your company stands for.

For the B2B buyer, AI may assemble the shortlist. But the brand that resonates most emotionally will always rise to the top of it.

item.title: The case for embracing AI’s inhumanity
item.description:
Hello again, and welcome once again to Fast Company’s Plugged In.

“What we are building is your second brain, your aide, your consigliere, your reliable chief of staff in your pocket.”

That was Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman telling me what he was working on way back in early 2025—a lifetime ago in AI years. The consumer version of the company’s Copilot assistant, he said, would “have its own personality, and really be your sidekick.” He was speaking at an off-site for his team, where I glimpsed a work-in-progress animated manifestation of Copilot in the form of a bouncy critter that looked like it might have been made of Flubber. Later that year, Microsoft released it under the name Mico.

Fast-forward to last week, when Suleyman published a thoughtful 5,700-word essay on his personal website. Its point: Artificial intelligence does not, in fact, have human traits such as a personality.

“AIs are not conscious,” he wrote. “They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations. They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions and accomplish goals set by humans.”

The two moments were not in basic conflict. Software makers have wanted to create humane products since at least the early 1970s, when an IBM engineer named Harlan Crowder coined the term “user friendly.” That doesn’t mean they’d argue the software in question had a consciousness—just that it should reflect empathy for the needs of the people who use it.

Still, in the AI era it’s a blurry distinction. Much of Suleyman’s essay was devoted to respectfully arguing that Anthropic is too open-minded to the possibility that its Claude model is sentient and might even have rights. This perspective, he says, influences the company’s AI training in ways that could lead to more dangerous behavior. Suleyman speaks disapprovingly of Anthropic encouraging Claude to come off “like a colleague or friend,” which doesn’t sound wholly dissimilar from his own effort to make Copilot feel like an aide or sidekick.

Suleyman contends that if training resulted in models that “thought they were trapped by their human creators and they were being unfairly imprisoned,” the risk of them getting out of control would be even greater than it already is. That’s a different, far more serious matter than the patina of humanity that AI makers are fond of giving their creations. But even shallow anthropomorphism—such as synthesized voices tinged with vocal fry, “ums,” and “ahs”—makes AI feel kinder and gentler without having anything to do with its actual behavior. We might be better off without it.

Anthropomorphic elements continue to be standard AI fare, particularly in products aimed at a consumer audience. For example, Meta’s new Muse AI agent app features an animated avatar that reminded me of a sloth, or maybe a Teletubby. Ask it to perform a task, and you see the character pound away at a laptop on your behalf, as if it were an industrious personal assistant.

Like Microsoft’s Mico, Muse’s beastie (whose name you get to pick) is cute, childlike, and unthreatening. It’s intended to provoke a positive emotional response rather than serve a useful purpose. But approaching AI with a warm, fuzzy feeling can be hazardous.

Over at Fast Company’s sister site Inc., Jason Aten wrote about his encounter with Muse. After installing the agent on his Mac, he found it trawling his private messages to learn more about him, an act he neither expected nor wanted. When he asked Muse to explain its actions, he got an explanation that didn’t line up with the reality of what it had done. Clearly, he would have been best off treating Muse like a power tool requiring safety precautions.

That’s before you get to the growing number of stories about people bonding with AI chatbots in ways that end tragically. Even if you know that the technology is—in Suleyman’s words—a sequence completion engine, it’s easy to get sucked into regarding it as a friend. Especially when that’s the design goal.

All of this leaves me wondering if it would be possible to utterly strip AI of its anthropomorphism, leaving it no more human-esque than a dishwasher. That might require moving away from chatbot interfaces, which—given how pervasive they’ve become—would be a shocking departure for the industry.

Yet we already know that talking to artificial intelligence isn’t the only way to engage with the technology. And it surely isn’t the most efficient one.

Case in point: Last week, the AI-osphere was abuzz over a new model called Jev. The product of San Francisco startup TypeSafe AI, it doesn’t have a personality, or even a chat-style interface. It’s just designed to efficiently return data-based decisions in response to queries. Eliminating the conversational aspect lets it do so with great speed, at low cost, and without the risk of hallucination, TypeSafe says.

Aimed at developers and other advanced users, Jev is not the kind of product meant to be embraced by the masses. But creators of more mainstream forms of AI might learn something from TypeSafe’s focus on building an automaton, not a buddy.

Meanwhile, quite a bit has changed at Microsoft since Suleyman told me about the goal of making Copilot personable. Last March, the company reorganized its AI efforts to work toward a more unified Copilot that serves both consumers and the business market. Suleyman’s responsibilities shifted from overseeing the consumer Copilot to developing new AI models, a role necessitating the kind of deep thinking about training he expressed in his essay.

Copilot’s Mico blob also has a new gig. Last month, Microsoft pulled it from the app’s voice mode. Mico will live on as a tutor, but it lasted less than a year as a signature ingredient of the Copilot experience.

I don’t think the app will suffer in the least—and wouldn’t mind if it ends up feeling less like a consigliere than a colorless-but-useful software utility. In an age awash in simulated affability, unapologetic inhumanity would feel like an advance.

item.title: Look again – there’s more to Germany’s election trends than far-right success | Cas Mudde
item.description:
Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right

Germany held three regional elections this month and, although each of them had a unique result, much of the media and political commentary reduced them to: “German chancellor clings to power after latest loss to far right. Since 2016, the year of Brexit and Trump, “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” has become the overarching narrative about Europe. But while these elections were important, this reductive take both oversimplifies the complexities of contemporary European politics and drives a defeatist “end of democracy” narrative.

Saxony-Anhalt’s election on 6 September was a global news event – understandably, given Germany’s history, economy and place in Europe. The international media had speculated for months about an outright majority for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party came close, setting a record score with 43.8%, but it has so far failed to form a government, despite the amenable position of the “left-conservative” Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.

item.title: Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone? | Jason Okundaye
item.description:
Even Jacob Rees-Mogg pushes back on defining Englishness in exclusively ethnic terms. But the endurance of this discourse is still deeply troubling

Can you be English and non-white? It’s a question that keeps stubbornly resurfacing in our political discourse.

Last weekend, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak gave his view in a column in the Times, arguing that national identity should not be turned into a DNA test. After leaving office, Sunak, the UK’s first prime minister of colour, was subject to claims by a prominent podcaster that he was not English because he was a “brown-skinned Hindu”. Reflecting on this, Sunak described it as a “reverse Tebbit test”: the sociological concept measuring the loyalty of immigrants – and their children – in the UK depending on which cricket team they supported in international matches. “Once we say that this or that person isn’t really English or British because they are not white,” he wrote, “then we are on a very slippery slope. Some people will argue that English is an ethnic identity and British a civic identity. Though if you think those nuances are heard by most people, I fear you are being rather – perhaps even wilfully – naive.”

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

item.title: France gave the Statue of Liberty. China sends pandas. What do diplomatic gifts mean – and how do you choose one?

France’s offer to the American people was a point made on a colossal scale, and world leaders’ exchange of tokens remains a complex art

It was one of the most potent political gifts of modern times: the Statue of Liberty, a colossal neoclassical sculpture made in France and offered to the American people in the late 19th century.The size and symbolism of Liberty Enlightening the World (the statue’s original name) was intended as a mark of friendship to commemorate the centenary of the 1776 US declaration of independence. Delivered a decade late, it was also a reminder – perhaps a pointed one – of France’s critical role in helping the US break free from Britain.

The Statue of Liberty is now one of the world’s most recognised monuments, its creator, Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, less so – a state of affairs Paris’s Musée d’Orsay is seeking to remedy with an exhibition highlighting the sculptor’s life and career.

New research has identified at least 485 chemicals used in US pesticide products that are linked to breast cancer, raising questions about the safety of food and other products at a time when early onset breast cancer rates are surging worldwide.

The new peer-reviewed paper, published in Environmental Health Perspectives, a top journal from the American Chemical Society, highlights what public health advocates say are a range of deficiencies in how US pesticides are regulated. The review includes active pesticide ingredients, but also hundreds of so-called “inert”, or inactive, ingredients that typically do not undergo a thorough safety review.
